content: Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster have released (preliminary versions of) three papers establishing finite time blowup (with smooth forcing term) for various fluid equations; not quite Navier-Stokes yet, but tantalizingly close, and with a clear mechanism: https://mathstodon.xyz/@tristanbuckmaster@mastodon.social/117233413735526010 . The proofs are formalized in Lean and verified with comparator at https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/fluid_lean . (It is all a rush job, for reasons explained in the mastodon post.)

I think the reasons explained for their rush (the first linked pdf on mastodon) should be read by all here. It suggests extremely unethical and coercive behavior by open AI.

EDIT : https://cims.nyu.edu/~tristanb/statement.pdf

Great reminder about how companies think about mathematics and mathematicians. I second Shreyas reccomendation of reading the statement.

I said that if OpenAI released its result in the way proposed I would go public with what happened. The reply was, “Why would you ruin your career?”
I don’t suppose “we reserve the right to gank your vibe proofs if they are cool enough” is in the TOS?

Wow, that's so dumb.

I actually believe it's plausible (uncertain whether it's likely) that OpenAI didn't actually "cheat" by taking anything from the transcripts of Tristan and Levent's suggestions, i.e. "all" they were doing was racing to scoop someone as the news started to leak. But the bullying is absolutely unacceptable.

Whether or not they cheated, isn't it a basic ethical principle with conflicts of interest that it's necessary to avoid the appearance of impropriety? That makes it a conflict of interest for OpenAI to both provide AI services for use in scientific research and to compete in research on the same problems or in the same fields, regardless of whether in fact confidential customer data is being used to compete with those customers. The fact that such conflicts are common in various kinds of marketplaces (providing a marketplace for third parties and also selling one's own competing products in that marketplace) doesn't make it any more ethical.

Could someone from OpenAI post their internal conflict of interest policy (or a link if it's already public) so we can see what if anything it says about avoiding competing with customers? If no such policy is available, or if OpenAI declines to disclose it, or if it doesn't exclude such competition with customers, or if a policy was only written long after AI became useful in research, we may make appropriate inferences.

In view of the speed with which AI companies like to rush things to go public and so to force others to rush, I suggest drawing adverse inferences is appropriate in the absence of full, public disclosures from OpenAI (regarding conflict of interest policies, policies on bullying, action taken against all staff involved in the reported bullying and conflicts of interest, etc.) by close of business today in California.

(Also, regarding the generous "racing to scoop" interpretation, having leaked information that approach X is helpful in tackling problem Y - not that many bits of information, not even fully reliable information - can provide an enormous advantage in constructing or reconstructing a solution, simply by motivating focusing work on that method, on that problem, at that time, rather than spending resources on other methods or problems or waiting until later.)

At least where I work, learning about a specific approach (idea/implementation etc), and then scooping the achievement would result in some serious academic consequences. We generally know that if someone has an idea it is theirs to publish. This relaxed atmosphere allows us to share our ideas and get feedback early on without worrying that we might get scooped.

It sounds like some people think there should be an ethical norm against a compute/inference provider competing with customers, regardless of if the provider uses confidential customer data or other "unfair" means of competition - I have genuinely never heard really heard this viewpoint before, so I would like to learn more about where this viewpoint comes from.

Here's my thoughts about "competing with customers" - I work for an edtech company, and we buy compute from AWS and tokens from OpenAI, Claude and Google, and I wouldn't really think of it as unethical for AWS/OpenAI/Anthropic/Google to release some educational app that competes directly with us. Indeed, I see it as a good thing that a grocery delivery startup, or a startup commercializing a relational database (say, spun out from some CS department), can buy cheap compute on AWS, in spite of the fact that the parent company offers Whole Foods delivery and RDS (a managed relational database).

The ethical norm, as I understand it, is simply that the platform cannot (for instance) use confidential customer data - and separately, if the customer hosts permissively-licencsed software (e.g. elasticsearch), some ethical debate about the effects of competition on the open source ecosystem (but, AIUI, those concerns would equally apply if, for e.g., it was Google who decided to compete with Elastic the company, not AWS). There is no norm that competing with customers is unethical per se. Indeed, if AWS declines to provide compute to that grocery delivery startup, some people might view that as unfair monopolistic behaviour, and hence unethical from that standpoint.

My thoughts for why this is a good norm is that it promotes "healthy" competition - startups benefit from being able to buy compute from a wide variety of cloud providers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft), and consumers benefit from having many grocery delivery choices, both from startups-who-get-cheap-compute and from big companies like Whole Foods - perhaps the economies of scale savings are more important to some consumers, and perhaps some consumers want some niche grocery delivery feature that a startup or small company is better suited to serve - the market can work it out.

(This is not a general defense of all the actions in question here, just my thoughts about "competing with customers")

While I (and a lot of anti-trust legislation) strongly disagree with this idea, maybe debating fair market competition is not in scope here unless it is connected to this specific instance where scientific work is involved; in which case CoI rules should be applied.

This is a Lean Zulip, so I'm going to ask a Lean specific question regarding these results. Let's say there will be two conceptually close formalizations published. Do we have tools (only lean based, not semantic understanding of markdown files) to figure out their subsets of overlap of theory? To estimate the duplicated cost of generating or compiling them in a duplicate? Dually, even if the terminal leaf statements are the same, can we identify where the built up theory diverges/differs? The same questions hold for FLT formalizations.

By way of analogy: suppose an OpenAI employee had their own AI startup business as a side hustle, and that business was making progress on similar AI problems to those OpenAI had recently been making progress on. The difficulties with formalizing Yang-Mills are mostly in the negative direction. I'd guess that a positive solution could be formalized. As for a negative solution, I'm not even sure what that would mean.

On the topic of the Hodge conjecture, if a counterexaple is found, will the paper be titled, "Hodge's conjecture is false for nontrivial reasons"?
If all the millennium problems fall this year or next, what is the next horizon?

As for Yang-Mills, one possible statement would be "there exists a set of correlation functions satisfying the Wightman/OS axioms and agreeing asymptotically with the perturbation theory". But the asymptotic part would be extremely long. If that could be reasonably written, the negation would be clear. (But for YM I would say that the expectation is a positive solution)

On the other hand, there could be a very specific construction. If a set of nongaussian correlation functions satisfying the OS axioms could be "extracted from" the continuum+infinite volume limit of the discretized YM and the two-point functions decay exponentially, I think everyone would regard it as a solution, without verifying the asymptotics. But here "extracted from" is too ambiguous. On the other hand, writing a specific way of "extraction" would be extremely long.

I believe that just writing either statement would be an important achievement.

It is perhaps worth noting that OS reconstruction is a route from Euclidean measures to a Hamiltonian theory with a spectrum condition. A potential solution could instead begin with the Hamiltonian structure and address the required axiomatic properties individually. So a general YM problem statement would need to cover that kind of approach as well.

If all the millennium problems fall this year or next, what is the next horizon?

I don't think of the Millennium problems as demarcating "the horizon." Math is enormous. The problems were selected because they make for good PR, not because they provide some kind of exhaustive list of the most important and difficult problems.

Millennium problems aside, I think the larger question is what the landscape will look like when AI models solve all the problems that they find easy. I firmly believe that the question, "Does conjecture C have a proof of length at most an exabyte?" is an intrinsically hard computational problem, so that no matter how good AI gets, there will always be problems that are hard for it. So there will always be an interesting frontier to explore at the outer limits of what we can prove. But exactly what that frontier will look like in ten years' time, nobody can predict right now.

At the time the millennium prizes were announced, there was some criticism from mathematicians that, as far as I know, did not make its way to the broader public. As I recall, the main complaints included:

  1. Mathematics isn't just about solving big questions, but the prize problems would encourage people to think so.
  2. The money would be better spent supporting younger mathematicians.
  3. The monetary prizes distort the existing incentive structures in mathematics.

The response was more or less "We think this is a good way to draw attention to important problems in various fields." I think they were successful in this goal, but perhaps the critics were also correct.
